heroCommands.comment: Serve a model with an OpenAI-compatible API

sixtySeconds.whatItDoes: vLLM is a Python library and server for running large language models efficiently. It loads open models from Hugging Face and serves them through an OpenAI-compatible API, so existing apps can switch to your own model with a URL change.
sixtySeconds.problem: Serving language models yourself is slow and memory-hungry if done naively. vLLM manages GPU memory carefully (its PagedAttention technique) and batches requests together so one GPU can answer many users at once.
whoFor: Teams self-hosting open models like Llama, Qwen or Gemma
Developers who want an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for their own model
ML engineers serving models at high throughput
Researchers running batched inference over large datasets
sixtySeconds.whyChoose: Choose it when you have a GPU server and want fast, production-style serving of open models. For running a model casually on a laptop, a desktop tool like Ollama is simpler.
requirements: Linux (macOS on Apple Silicon via vLLM-Metal)
A supported GPU (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) or CPU, with enough memory for your model

overview: vLLM started at UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab and is now maintained by a large community of companies and universities. It is a library for LLM inference and serving: you point it at a model on Hugging Face and it runs it, either in a Python script or as a web server.

The server speaks the OpenAI API (plus the Anthropic Messages API and gRPC), so tools and SDKs built for OpenAI work against it. The README lists support for more than 200 model architectures, including Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, multimodal models and embedding models.

Its speed comes from PagedAttention memory management, continuous batching of requests, prefix caching, quantization (FP8, INT8, INT4, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and more) and optimized GPU kernels. It also supports tool calling, structured output, multi-LoRA and spreading a model across several GPUs.

features.title: OpenAI-compatible server
features.body: vllm serve exposes chat and completion endpoints that work with the OpenAI SDK and tools.

features.title: Hundreds of models
features.body: Runs 200+ model architectures from Hugging Face, including multimodal and embedding models.

features.title: High throughput
features.body: PagedAttention and continuous batching let one GPU serve many requests at once.

features.title: Quantization
features.body: Run smaller, faster versions of models with FP8, INT8, INT4, GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF and more.

features.title: Multi-GPU and distributed
features.body: Tensor, pipeline, data and expert parallelism for models too big for one GPU.

features.title: Broad hardware support
features.body: NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, x86/ARM/PowerPC CPUs, plus plugins for TPUs and other chips.

strengths: Widely used, very active project with a large community
Drop-in OpenAI API replacement for your own models
Strong performance for serving many users
Apache-2.0 license, fine for commercial use
limitations: Linux is the main supported OS; macOS needs the separate vLLM-Metal plugin
The server hosts one model at a time
You need a GPU with enough memory for the model you choose
More setup than desktop tools aimed at casual local use

install.verificationNote: Commands come from vLLM's README and quickstart guide. AIRepoHub hasn't run them yet.

steps.title: Install vLLM
steps.body: --torch-backend=auto picks the right PyTorch build for your CUDA driver.

steps.title: Download precompiled kernels
steps.body: Optional, but avoids several minutes of compiling at startup on newer GPUs.

environment.name: VLLM_API_KEY
environment.description: Set this (or pass --api-key) to make the server require an API key.

environment.name: UV_TORCH_BACKEND
environment.description: Choose a specific PyTorch backend, for example cu126, instead of auto-detection.

tutorial.title: Serve an open model with an OpenAI-compatible API
tutorial.useCase: Run Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on your own GPU and call it like the OpenAI API.
setup: A Linux machine with a supported GPU

steps.title: Start the server
steps.body: It listens on http://localhost:8000 by default.

steps.title: Send a chat request

tutorial.expected: The server downloads the model from Hugging Face, starts on port 8000, and answers the chat request in the same JSON format as the OpenAI API.
nextSteps: Point the OpenAI Python SDK at http://localhost:8000/v1 to use it from code
Use the LLM class in Python for offline batch inference

costs.label: License
costs.value: Apache-2.0. Free to use, modify and use commercially.

costs.label: Hardware
costs.value: You need your own GPU machine or a cloud GPU, which can cost money per hour.

costs.label: Models
costs.value: Open models on Hugging Face are free to download; check each model's license.

troubleshooting.solution: Run vllm download-kernels after installing to use precompiled kernels instead of compiling them at startup.

troubleshooting.problem: Wrong PyTorch or CUDA build installed
troubleshooting.solution: Install with --torch-backend=auto, or set a specific backend such as --torch-backend=cu126.

troubleshooting.problem: Answers differ from what you expect
troubleshooting.solution: The server applies the model's generation_config.json by default. Pass --generation-config vllm to turn that off.
Use vLLM-Metal for Apple Silicon; see the GPU installation guide's Apple Silicon tab.

bestFor: Self-hosting open language models on GPUs
